definition: To show or prove that a decision or action is right or reasonable.
example: Can you justify spending the club's entire budget on a single printer?
nuance: To justify an action is to argue that it was right, while to excuse it is to ask that a fault be forgiven.
prompt: A student asks her teacher for an extension on a research paper.
options: She tried to justify her request by showing a note about the library's delayed books.
She decided to justify the deadline by moving it two weeks later on her own.
To justify her request, she cheerfully admitted that she had no reason at all for needing more time.
Her teacher will justify the paper with a grade of B-plus.
reasons: Offering evidence that the delay was beyond her control gives a good reason for the request.
Changing a date yourself is adjusting it, not giving reasons that support it.
Admitting there is no reason weakens the request instead of supporting it.
Assigning a grade is evaluating work, not defending a choice with reasons.

practice.prompt: A town council is debating whether to pay for a new bridge.
options: A resident tried to justify the project by listing every single way it would waste the town's money.
Workers will justify the bridge by bolting its steel beams into place.
The engineer's report helped justify the cost by showing the old bridge was cracking.
The council voted to justify pale gray as the color for the railings.
reasons: Listing drawbacks argues against a project rather than for it.
Putting up a structure is construction; this verb involves argument or evidence.
Proof that the old bridge is unsafe makes the spending look sensible.
Picking a color is choosing, not giving reasons that a choice is sound.
